items.stimulus: Pteropods, often called sea butterflies, are snails that have abandoned the seafloor. Over millions of years, the muscular foot that a garden snail uses to creep has evolved in pteropods into two thin flaps, which the animals beat to "fly" through open water. Many species are smaller than a lentil. Some feed by releasing a web of mucus several times their body width and then reeling it in along with the plankton caught in it. Pteropods are in turn a major food source for fish such as salmon and mackerel.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how pteropods use mucus webs to capture plankton
To argue that pteropods deserve more study from marine scientists
To describe a group of tiny snails that live in open water
To show that pteropods move in much the same way garden snails do
items.explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. Each one gives a fact about pteropods: how they swim, how small they are, how they feed and what eats them. Together they profile a group of small snails that live in open water. The text only informs, so the neutral verb "describe" fits, and the choice covers the whole passage rather than one detail.

B.why: You chose a verb that is too strong. The text never gives an opinion or says pteropods need more research. It only presents facts, so "argue" claims more than the passage does.

D.why: You reversed the comparison the text makes. The passage says the foot a garden snail uses to creep has evolved in pteropods into flaps for swimming. That is a difference between the two animals, not a similarity.

Rather than shading mountains in uniform gray, Ferrand blended soft greens, browns, and violets so that slopes facing the morning sun appeared lighter than those in shadow. Rather than relying on government surveys, she rode buses with work crews before dawn and wrote down what each worker earned that day. Her handwritten ledgers, now held at a university library, are among the most detailed wage records from the period. items.stimulus: In the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, western hemlocks often stand in straight rows, their roots arching over empty space. Each row marks where a fallen tree once lay: seedlings sprouted on the rotting trunk, and when it decayed, the young trees were left standing on stilts. Ecologists call such trunks nurse logs. Why seedlings favor them was long unclear, but ecologist Mara Lindqvist found that seedlings planted on bare forest floor survived well when moss was cleared away, suggesting that logs help mainly by raising seedlings above smothering moss.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe a forest pattern and present a finding about what causes it
To explain how the roots of some hemlocks come to arch over empty space
To show that rotting logs give seedlings nutrients the forest floor lacks
To argue that clearing moss from forests would improve tree regeneration
items.explanation: The text first describes a pattern (rows of hemlocks on stilts, grown from nurse logs). It then raises an open question (why do seedlings favor logs?) and answers it with Lindqvist's finding (logs lift seedlings above the moss). The right purpose has to cover both halves.

B.why: The text does explain the stilt roots, but only in its second sentence. This choice covers the opening and leaves out the question and the study that take up the second half.

C.why: The name 'nurse log' suggests nourishment, but the study points the other way. Seedlings did well on bare ground once the moss was gone, so the benefit is height, not nutrients.

D.why: The finding is about why seedlings survive on logs, and the text recommends nothing. 'Argue' and a forest-management proposal go well past an explanation of one natural pattern.

items.stimulus: When the Orrin Street Viaduct opened in 1928, newspapers celebrated its length: at 1.4 kilometers, it was the longest concrete span in the region. As engineering historian Lena Okafor notes, however, the viaduct's lasting influence came from something few visitors noticed. Its designer, Ruth Calloway, divided the deck into short segments separated by joints packed with tarred felt, allowing the concrete to swell and shrink with the seasons without cracking. Within a decade, the approach had become standard on bridges across the country.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To report the length that made the viaduct the longest concrete span in its region
To argue that newspapers praised the viaduct for a feature engineers thought trivial
To explain how felt-packed joints let concrete swell and shrink without cracking
To describe a bridge and point to an overlooked feature behind its influence
items.explanation: The text turns on 'however.' The bridge's famous feature (its length) is set aside for the feature that actually made it influential (the segmented deck and its joints), and the last sentence confirms that influence. The right choice names both the bridge and the overlooked feature.

A.why: The length is the setup that the 'however' turns away from. You picked a true detail from the first sentence instead of the point the text moves to.

B.why: You caught the contrast, but the text never says engineers thought the length was trivial or that the newspapers were wrong. It says the bridge's lasting influence came from elsewhere. 'Argue' and 'trivial' make that contrast harsher than the text does.

C.why: This is how the joints work, which is one sentence of the passage. It leaves out the viaduct, the contrast with its fame, and the influence that is the reason the joints are mentioned at all.

items.stimulus: Most surviving records of eighteenth-century weaving were kept by mill owners, who noted output and wages but rarely the cloth itself. The pattern book of Agnes Muir, a handloom weaver in Paisley, Scotland, is a rare exception. Across 212 pages, Muir pasted a snippet of every cloth she wove beside the threading draft used to produce it, and she annotated failures as carefully as successes. A craft's knowledge often survives only where a practitioner chose to write it down. Historians now use Muir's book to reconstruct techniques that no mill ledger describes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To claim that craft knowledge survives only when practitioners write it down
To present a weaver's record and explain why it matters to historians of the craft
To describe how one weaver arranged cloth samples alongside her threading drafts
To argue that mill owners deliberately left weavers' techniques out of their records
items.explanation: The text sets out a gap (mill records ignore the cloth), introduces Muir's book as the exception, describes what the book contains, and ends with how historians use it. 'Present' a record and 'explain why it matters' covers each of those steps.

A.why: You picked out the one general sentence, but you changed its 'often' to 'only' and treated it as the main claim. In the passage it is a comment on Muir's book, not the claim the book is offered to support.

C.why: The text does say how the samples and drafts were arranged, but that is a description of the book's contents. It leaves out why the book matters, which the first and last sentences make the point.

D.why: The text says mill owners 'rarely' recorded the cloth. It says nothing about why. 'Deliberately' adds a motive, and 'argue' adds an accusation, and neither is in the text.

items.stimulus: For decades, archivists catalogued Henrik Dahl's 1868 map of the Vessa delta as an unfinished draft. Many of its channels are drawn only in dotted lines, and several islands appear twice, in slightly different positions. A reexamination by cartographic historian Priya Natarajan suggests the map is complete. Comparing it with Dahl's field notes, she found that the dotted channels hold water only during spring floods and that the doubled islands mark where sandbars stood in summer and in winter. Dahl, it appears, mapped a landscape that would not stay still.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To present a reinterpretation of a map's odd features as a record of seasonal change
To criticize archivists for carelessly cataloguing a complete map as an unfinished draft
To explain why the sandbars of a river delta shifted position between summer and winter
To urge that other maps catalogued as drafts be reexamined using surveyors' field notes
items.explanation: The text starts with an old belief (the map was unfinished), names the features behind that belief (dotted channels, doubled islands), and then gives Natarajan's correction: those features record seasonal change. The verb 'present' fits the text's measured tone ('suggests,' 'it appears').

B.why: You saw that the archivists were wrong, which is right, but the text never blames them. Being mistaken isn't the same as being careless, and 'criticize' needs an opinion that the text's neutral tone doesn't show.

C.why: The text says that the sandbars moved with the seasons, not why they did. The movement is the explanation for the map's features, not the subject of the passage.

D.why: The text deals with one map and makes no recommendation. Turning one reexamination into a call to review other maps adds a prescription the passage never makes.

items.stimulus: Hydrologists have long known that a stream's flow rises after rain, but it has been unclear how much of that rise is new rainwater and how much is older groundwater pushed out by it. Hydrologist Daniel Osei set out to test this in a small Welsh catchment. Because rain and groundwater carry slightly different ratios of oxygen isotopes, he could track each source in the stream. During storms, he found, more than two-thirds of the water in the channel had been underground for weeks before the rain fell.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how oxygen isotopes distinguish rainwater from groundwater in streams
To argue that rainfall has little effect on the amount of water a stream carries
To show that in all catchments, storm water in streams is mostly old groundwater
To report a finding about where the water that swells a stream during storms comes from
items.explanation: The text poses a question (is storm flow new rain or old groundwater?), describes how Osei tested it, and gives the answer (mostly old groundwater). 'Report a finding about where the water comes from' covers the question, the method and the result without saying more than the single study shows.

A.why: The isotope method is only how the question was answered, and it takes up one sentence. This choice leaves out the question and the result.

B.why: Once you see that most storm water is old, it's tempting to conclude that rain doesn't matter. But the text starts by saying flow rises after rain. The rain still causes the rise; it does so by pushing out groundwater.

C.why: You read the result correctly, then spread it to 'all catchments.' Osei studied one small catchment in Wales, so the text can't support a universal claim.

items.stimulus: Divers have long regarded the pistol shrimp as little more than a source of noise: the snap of its oversized claw, loud enough to interfere with sonar, crackles across warm reefs. Marine biologist Keiko Arai has documented a less obvious side of the animal. The shrimp dig burrows in reef sediment and share them with gobies, small fish that watch for predators while the nearly blind shrimp maintain the tunnels. In Arai's survey plots, the burrows also aerated sediment to a depth of half a meter, sustaining worms and clams that sheltered there.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how the pistol shrimp's claw makes a snap loud enough to disrupt sonar
To describe the partnership in which gobies stand guard while shrimp dig tunnels
To present overlooked ways in which an animal known for its noise supports reef life
To argue that the pistol shrimp does more good than harm to the reefs it inhabits
items.explanation: The text sets up the common view (the shrimp is mostly a noise), then turns to 'a less obvious side' and gives two examples: the shared burrows with gobies, and burrows that aerate sediment for worms and clams. 'Overlooked ways' covers both examples, and 'present' matches the informational tone.

A.why: The snap belongs to the old view that the text moves away from, and the text never explains how the claw produces it. You fixed on the first sentence.

B.why: The goby partnership is real and in the text, but it is only the first of two examples. The choice leaves out the aeration finding and the contrast with the shrimp's reputation, so it is too narrow.

D.why: You saw the shift from nuisance to benefit, then turned it into a verdict. The text never compares the shrimp's harms with its benefits, and the word 'argue' needs an opinion the text doesn't state.
